terms.gloss: don’t do it! don’t do that!
terms.grammar: nē with the perfect subjunctive, the classical prohibition
evidence: Plaut. Men. 414–415: Hercle opīnor, pernegārī nōn potest. — Nē fēcerīs.
Plin. Ep. 1.18.5: Quod dubitēs, nē fēcerīs.
terms.comment: What Plautus’s people say to stop someone on the point of doing a thing, and the form of the old rule of the cautious that Pliny quotes. The perfect subjunctive has a long ī: fēcerīs. See “don’t!” for the constructions in general.

evidence: Plaut. Most. 813: nōlī facere mentiōnem tē hās ēmisse
Plaut. Merc. 934: nōlī istuc quaesō dīcere
terms.comment: The plain nōlī form, gentler than Nē fēcerīs. We have found it with an object or another verb (nōlī facere mentiōnem, nōlī istuc dīcere), not as nōlī istuc facere itself, which is ours on that model.

phrases.english: Don’t do that, son; it’ll break.

phrases.latin: Hercle opīnor, pernegārī nōn potest. — Nē fēcerīs: periistī, sī intrāssis intrā līmen.
phrases.english: By Hercules, I think it can’t be denied. — Don’t do it: you’re done for if you step over that threshold.

phrases.latin: Stultus es; nōlī istuc quaesō dīcere.
phrases.english: You’re being silly; please don’t say that.

sources: Lewis & Short: ne · Lewis & Short: facio · Lewis & Short: nolo
